subject: English
summaryPoints: Adverbial clauses of comparison establish equality (as...as / not so...as), superiority/inferiority (-er / more...than), or absolute maximum within a set (-est / the most...of/in).

Conditional sentences span four core models: Zero conditional (general/scientific truths: If + present, present), Type 1 (realistic/probable future: If + present, will + V1), Type 2 (unreal/hypothetical present: If + past/were, would + V1), and Type 3 (counterfactual past: If + had + V3, would have + V3).
The subordinating conjunction 'unless' functions as an equivalent to 'if...not'; therefore, the clause introduced by 'unless' must not contain an additional negative word.
Conditional inversion creates formal elevated style by omitting 'if' and placing the auxiliary first: Type 1 uses 'Should you...', Type 2 uses 'Were I...', and Type 3 uses 'Had I + V3...'.

Consonant phonemes are classified according to manner and place of articulation: dental fricatives contrast voiceless /θ/ (think, math, tenth) with voiced /ð/ (this, father, them); nasal consonants block oral airflow and emit air nasally (/m/, /n/, /ŋ/); and affricates release plosive closure into friction (/tʃ/ and /dʒ/).

Preferences are expressed through distinctive syntax: 'prefer + gerund/noun + to + gerund/noun', 'would prefer + to-infinitive + rather than + bare infinitive', and 'would rather + bare infinitive + than + bare infinitive'.

formulas.label: Inversion of Conditional Type 3 Formula
formulas.expr: Had + Subject + V3(past participle) + , + Subject + would / could / might + have + V3(past participle)

formulas.label: Inversion of Conditional Type 1 & 2 Formulas
formulas.expr: Type 1: Should + Subject + V1(base) + , + Subject + will + V1  |  Type 2: Were + Subject + (to + V1) + , + Subject + would + V1

formulas.label: Negative Conditional Equivalence Formula
formulas.expr: Unless + Subject + Affirmative Verb + , + Main Clause  =  If + Subject + Negative Verb + , + Main Clause

formulas.label: Preference Syntax Formulas
formulas.expr: Subject + prefer + V-ing + to + V-ing  |  Subject + would rather + V1(base) + than + V1(base)  |  Subject + would prefer + to-V1 + rather than + V1

examTip: Inverted conditionals are extremely common on the EUEE. When an inverted conditional begins with 'Had', verify that the if-less clause contains a past participle (e.g., 'Had I known the truth...'), and that the main clause contains 'would have + V3' (NOT just 'would + V1'). Also remember: 'would rather' is followed by a bare infinitive, while 'prefer' is followed by 'to'.

keyDefinitions.definition: The formal syntactic omission of the conjunction 'if' accomplished by inverting the auxiliary verb (had, were, should) to the sentence-initial position before the subject.
A consonant sound produced by positioning the tip or blade of the tongue against the upper teeth, producing voiceless /θ/ or voiced /ð/.
A consonant sound produced by lowering the velum and completely occluding oral airflow, allowing sound and air to resonate through the nasal cavity (/m/, /n/, /ŋ/).
A complex consonant phoneme that begins as a complete stop/plosive and releases as a grooved fricative at the same point of articulation (/tʃ/, /dʒ/).

eueeFocusTopics: Inversion of conditional clauses (Had + S + V3, Were + S, Should + S)
Conditional sentences Type 0, 1, 2, and 3 structural matching
Formulas for expressing preference: 'prefer...to' versus 'would rather...than'
Phonetic minimal pairs: dental fricatives (/θ/ vs /ð/) and nasals (/n/ vs /ŋ/)
